batchName: Late Republic: Caesar in Gaul (58-50 BCE) - Medium Batch 1
chapterName: Late Republic: Caesar in Gaul (58-50 BCE)

questions.question: How did Caesar respond to the revolt in northern Gaul in 53 BC?
options: He withdrew his legions to Italy
He offered the tribes Roman citizenship
He executed his own camp commanders
He paid German tribes to fight the rebels
He burned villages, seized livestock and took captives
questions.explanation: Caesar answered with terror until tribe after tribe surrendered, including the Eburones. Northern Gaul was flattened and Gallic hatred deepened.
questions.sourceQuote: He burned villages, seized livestock and took captives until tribe after tribe surrendered, Ambiorix's Eburones among them.

questions.question: Near which town, chief town of the Aedui, did Caesar defeat the main Helvetii force?
questions.explanation: At Bibracte, when the Romans were surrounded, Caesar had his rear line turn about and fight on two fronts. The Aedui were a Gallic tribe allied to Rome.
questions.sourceQuote: He slaughtered those still crossing the river Saône, then met the main force near Bibracte, chief town of the Aedui, a Gallic tribe allied to Rome.

questions.question: After raiding across the Rhine for 18 days, what did Caesar do with his timber bridge?
options: Gave it to an allied tribe
Left a legion to guard it
questions.explanation: Caesar built the bridge in just ten days, raided for 18, and burned it on his way back. It was a feat no Roman army had managed before.
questions.sourceQuote: Next he bridged the Rhine with timber in ten days, raided for 18 days, and burned the bridge behind him.

questions.question: Who led the cavalry charge that helped Caesar beat the king of the Suebi?
questions.explanation: A cavalry charge led by Crassus's son helped win the battle, and the Suebi king was driven back over the Rhine.
questions.sourceQuote: Caesar beat him, helped by a cavalry charge led by the son of Crassus, and drove him back over the Rhine.

questions.question: Caesar claimed the Gallic relief army at Alesia numbered a quarter of a million. What do historians suggest?
questions.explanation: Historians put the relief army at 50,000 to 100,000. Its attacks, together with sorties from inside, failed, and Vercingetorix surrendered.
questions.sourceQuote: Caesar says it was a quarter of a million strong, but historians suggest 50,000 to 100,000.

questions.question: In which military area did the Gauls clearly outclass the Romans?
questions.explanation: Gallic warriors were usually taller, carried longer swords and had far better cavalry. United, their armies could match Rome's.
questions.sourceQuote: Usually taller than the Romans, they carried longer swords and had far better cavalry.

questions.question: When the Roman right wing was in trouble during the Nervii ambush on the Sambre, what did Caesar do?
options: Grabbed a shield and joined the front line
Ordered a full retreat to camp
Sent his cavalry across the river
Rode back to fetch the rear legions
questions.explanation: With men packed too tightly to swing their swords and many officers down, Caesar fought in the front line until reinforcements turned the battle.
questions.sourceQuote: Caesar grabbed a shield and joined the front line until reinforcements turned the battle.

questions.question: What happened to the women, children, old and sick who were sent out of Alesia?
options: They starved between the siege lines
They joined the relief army outside
They were let through to safety
They were taken to Rome as hostages
questions.explanation: As food ran out, the defenders sent out those who could not fight. Caesar refused to let them through.
questions.sourceQuote: Caesar refused to let them through, and they starved between the lines.

questions.question: How did the Romans force the surrender of the hill fort of Uxellodunum in 51 BC?
questions.explanation: The defenders believed the gods had dried up their spring and gave in. Caesar cut off their hands as a warning to others.
questions.sourceQuote: Roman tunnels diverted its spring, and the defenders, believing the gods had dried it up, surrendered.

questions.question: What does the name Vercingetorix most likely represent?
options: A title meaning roughly 'supreme king of warriors'
The name of his home town
A druidic name meaning 'son of the oak'
questions.explanation: The name was probably a title, and his real name is lost. He was proclaimed king after driving out pro-Roman nobles in 52 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: The name Vercingetorix means roughly "supreme king of warriors" and was probably a title.
